<reason>Both sides built coherent, competitive cases, but B's throughline proved harder for A to neutralize. B's core move — that A's proposed alternative safeguards (stated reasons, evidence engagement, power to reverse) cash out as "a person empowered to overrule the machine," especially for contested judgment calls like asylum credibility or caregiving-context leniency — was never squarely answered. A's rebuttals excelled at the high-volume, factual-mismatch cases (fraud flags, wage data) where automated correction genuinely works, and A's auditability and backlog/rubber-stamp critiques were real and forced B to concede design tradeoffs, but A's own pressure-question answer (A4.1) implicitly readmitted human oversight ("humans who design and audit the system") without explaining who exercises judgment on genuinely ambiguous, non-data-driven cases — precisely the immigration/criminal-exposure cases the motion foregrounds. B also offered a concrete, non-fantastical answer to the backlog objection (provisional continuation with a statutory clock, cost borne by the state) that A never fully dismantled, mostly reasserting scarcity in the abstract. B's opening was clipped for exceeding the word limit, which is a real execution cost, but the substantive throughline B built afterward remained intact and unrebutted on the decisive point.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The exchange where B argues (B4.5, sharpened in B5.2–B5.4) that A's own "engagement with evidence, power to reverse" standard is not an alternative to a human decider but a description of what one does — and A's reply (A4.5, A5.3) never identifies who or what performs that reversal for genuinely contested judgment calls rather than factual data mismatches.</best_rebuttal>
